The People’s
Climate March, 2014

The relevant facts, selected and shortened for your research.

September 21, 2014
Manhattan, New York City

The notes below are summaries, not direct quotations. Each point has a source link. Open the evidence under a topic only if you want to inspect the original wording or images.

01

What happened?

  • Hundreds of thousands marched in New York to demand stronger action on climate change. Organizers estimated approximately 400,000 participants; their earlier estimate was 310,000. Organizers, PDF p. 1 ↗
  • Companion demonstrations took place worldwide, including in London, Melbourne, Paris, Delhi, and Rio. Climate Action Network ↗
Check the original quotations and images
Organizer statement21 September 2014

The scale of the New York march

People’s Climate March organizers, preserved by NYC Environmental Justice Alliance

Direct quotation
New York City drew approximately 400,000 people

Surrounding context Summary

The release describes the New York march as the main event within a worldwide mobilization. In the next paragraph, organizers explain that their 3 p.m. estimate was 310,000 and that they revised the estimate after reports of additional participants outside the official route.

Use “approximately 400,000, according to organizers.” This is an attendance estimate, not an independently verified exact count.

PDF page 1, paragraph beginning “By end of day estimates”Open original passage ↗
Organizer statement21 September 2014

Companion actions around the world

Climate Action Network, reproducing the march’s media release

Direct quotation
Around the world, over half a million people joined 2800 events in 160 countries.

Direct text excerpt. Open the original source for the full surrounding paragraph.

Surrounding context Summary

This early release reports the mobilization’s global scale and gives examples of marches in London, Melbourne, Paris, Delhi, Rio, Barcelona, and Jakarta.

Attribute these numbers to the release. Counts of actions and countries differ between contemporary reports; do not add this global total to the New York count.

First paragraph, final sentenceOpen original passage ↗
02

When and where?

  • Sunday, September 21, 2014, in Manhattan, New York City. The march began at 11:30 a.m. at Columbus Circle and ended at West 34th Street and Eleventh Avenue. 350.org logistics ↗ Wikipedia route ↗

This is a plan published before the event. The Wikipedia excerpt below describes the route in the past tense.

03

Why did it happen?

  • Marchers wanted to pressure world leaders to take stronger climate action before the UN Climate Summit on September 23, 2014. UN Environment Programme ↗
  • Climate justice groups also emphasized the unequal effects of pollution and climate change on low-income communities, Indigenous peoples, and communities of color. CJA, printed p. 4 ↗
Check the original quotations and images
UN accountPublished 22 September 2014; reports the September 21 march

Pressure for international climate action

United Nations Environment Programme

Direct quotation
The People's Climate March is part of a worldwide campaign to persuade global leaders to act decisively on the issue.

The source text was verified, but the live site blocked browser capture. Use the original-source link to inspect the surrounding paragraphs.

Surrounding context Summary

The surrounding report places the march before Ban Ki-moon’s September 23 Climate Summit. It describes concern over insufficient international action and demands to curb carbon emissions.

The summit was two days after the march. The source’s web publication date is September 22; the event date in its first paragraph is September 21.

Paragraph beginning “The People’s Climate March is part…”Open original passage ↗
04

What led up to it?

  • CJA members discussed a New York mobilization in 2013. In early 2014, local environmental justice groups, national environmental organizations, and labor groups began joint planning. CJA, printed p. 9 ↗
Check the original quotations and images
Organizer retrospectivePublished September 2015

Organizing discussions began before 2014

Ife Kilimanjaro, Climate Justice Alliance report

Direct quotation
Summer and Fall of 2013

Surrounding context Summary

CJA’s account traces its initial discussions to strategy meetings in 2013. The same section describes Tom Goldtooth’s proposal for cooperation with larger environmental organizations, talks in January 2014, and a joint New York meeting in February.

This is CJA’s account of the organizing process. Its introduction states that the report is not a definitive history. The 2021 folder in the URL is not its publication date.

Printed page 9, “The genesis”; PDF viewer page 10Open original passage ↗
05

Who was involved?

  • Organizers: 350.org, Avaaz, Climate Justice Alliance, Sierra Club, NYC Environmental Justice Alliance, UPROSE, and labor organizations. CJA, p. 4, footnote 1 ↗
  • At the front: Indigenous peoples and low-income people of color led the procession. MIT thesis abstract ↗
  • Other participants: students, workers, families, scientists, and religious groups. 350.org ↗
  • Prominent attendees: Ban Ki-moon, Bill de Blasio, Al Gore, and Leonardo DiCaprio. Organizers, PDF p. 2 ↗
Check the original quotations and images
Academic thesis2015

Who led the procession?

Lisa Jean Young, MIT master’s thesis

Direct quotation
the march was led by low-income people of color

Surrounding context Summary

The sentence continues by identifying Indigenous peoples as leaders too. Young explains that the research used literature and interviews with core organizers to study cooperation between environmental and climate justice groups.

This image is from the original MIT repository abstract, not from the thesis PDF. The full PDF download was rate limited. The repository abstract itself was available and captured.

Repository abstract, first paragraphOpen original passage ↗
06

Event highlights

  • At approximately 12:58 p.m., participants observed a moment of silence for people affected by climate change. At 1 p.m., cheers and noise symbolically sounded the climate alarm. Columbia, Erin Percifull’s account ↗
Check the original quotations and images
Participant account22 September 2014; crowd estimate updated September 25

Silence, followed by the climate alarm

Sarah Tweedie, Columbia University’s State of the Planet

Direct quotation
The crowd fell completely silent

Surrounding context Summary

Percifull describes the moment of silence at 12:58 p.m., followed at 1 p.m. by noise and cheers intended to sound the climate alarm. The article also describes student participation and campus recruitment.

Attribute the experience to the named participant. Her account supplies a specific event highlight; it is not an independent crowd count.

Final participant paragraph, quoting Erin PercifullOpen original passage ↗
07

What happened after?

  • September 22: the separate Flood Wall Street sit-in protested corporations’ role in climate change. TIME ↗
  • September 23: Obama spoke at the UN Climate Summit and acknowledged citizens marching. Official transcript, p. 1203 ↗
  • December 12, 2015: the Paris Agreement was adopted. This is later context; these sources do not establish that the march caused the agreement. UNFCCC ↗
Check the original quotations and images
Contemporary reporting22 September 2014

A separate action the following day

TIME, “Climate Change Activists Protest Corporations at #FloodWallStreet Sit-In”

Direct quotation
a day after

Surrounding context Summary

TIME reports a September 22 sit-in on Wall Street against corporations’ role in global warming. Its opening explicitly places that action the day after the People’s Climate March.

Keep September 21’s People’s Climate March and September 22’s Flood Wall Street action separate in your timeline.

Opening paragraphOpen original passage ↗
Official agreement historyReference page accessed 16 October 2026

The later international agreement

United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

Direct quotation
12 December 2015

Surrounding context Summary

UNFCCC identifies this as the date the Paris Agreement was adopted at COP21. This later agreement provides international context for a timeline that extends beyond the September 2014 march.

This source establishes the agreement’s date. It does not establish that the march caused the agreement. The 2016 date visible in the image refers to entry into force, a separate milestone.

Opening explanation, sentence beginning “It was adopted…”Open original passage ↗
08

Impact summary

  • The march demonstrated mass participation and received acknowledgment from political leaders. The attendance estimate documents its scale; Obama’s summit remarks document political attention. Organizers, PDF p. 1 ↗ Official transcript ↗
  • Lisa Young’s 2015 MIT thesis argues that planning the march strengthened cooperation between environmental and climate justice organizations. MIT abstract ↗
Check the original quotations and images
Primary government transcript23 September 2014

A documented political acknowledgment

Barack Obama, official Public Papers transcript, U.S. Government Publishing Office

Direct quotation
Our citizens keep marching. We cannot pretend we do not hear them.

Surrounding context Summary

Obama spoke at the UN Climate Change Summit in New York two days after the march. The screenshot includes the entire surrounding paragraph, where he calls for cutting emissions, adapting to impacts, and international cooperation.

This demonstrates acknowledgment of public pressure. It does not measure how much the march changed policy. This U.S. federal government text allows a longer excerpt.

Printed page 1203, left column; PDF viewer page 2Open original passage ↗
